title: Like an infant
hookLine: can you soften your breath like a baby's? give birth without possessing (Tao Te Ching 10)
last: WHEN THE WORK IS DONE, STEP BACK.

cards: A baby asleep on a parent's chest. Watch the belly, not the face. It rises, it falls, and nothing else in the body seems to be helping or fighting.
No clenched jaw. No shoulders up near the ears. Now check your own breath, right where it is, without fixing it.
Is it soft, or is it working? Chapter ten of the Tao Te Ching holds up that sleeping baby as a kind of teacher, and this chapter doesn't instruct. It asks.

teach.b: First, a string of questions. Can you hold body and spirit together, and not let them drift apart? Can you gather your breath and make it soft, like an infant's?
Can you wipe your inner sight clean? Can you care for people without cleverness? The chapter doesn't answer them.
They're left open, like a hard question left on the board overnight. Second, why an infant?

teach.h: A BABY HASN'T LEARNED TO BRACE.
teach.b: A baby hasn't learned to brace yet, to hold its breath before a hard conversation or tighten up in traffic.

The softness isn't a technique it practiced; it simply hasn't been trained out of it. The chapter seems to ask whether a grown person can find their way back to that, on purpose. Third, softness isn't weakness.
Two days ago, chapter eight praised water for doing good without competing. A soft breath has the same quiet strength, small enough to carry in your own chest. Fourth, from breath to what you make.

teach.h: GIVE LIFE, AND DON'T POSSESS IT.
teach.b: The chapter closes with a list: to give life and not possess it, to act and not lean on it, to lead and not control. The book calls this a hidden kind of virtue.
A parent knows its shape: you raise a child, and the child is not yours to own.

teach.h: CAN YOU MAKE YOUR BREATH SOFT?
teach.b: The soft breath and the open hand sit side by side in the same chapter.

how: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching pair chapter ten with a few minutes of quiet, unforced breathing, letting the breath move on its own instead of controlling it.

o: helpless, needing someone else to decide
soft and unbraced, the way a baby breathes

p: a breath that hasn't learned to brace

s: chapter ten is a list of commands
it's a list of questions, and the book leaves them open.
the chapter's ending is about giving without possessing
to give life and not possess it, act and not lean on it, lead and not control.
soft breath means breathing as slowly and deeply as you can
today's practice asked only for softness: in without pulling, out without pushing.

games.q: chapter ten asks: can you make your breath soft, like an infant's? how does the book answer its own question?
o: it says yes, and gives a method.
it doesn't answer; it leaves the question open.
games.why: the chapter is a string of questions with no answers given. the listener is left to try.

practice: Sit or lie down with one hand on your belly, and let the breath come in without pulling and go out without pushing.

Not slow, not deep, only soft, like the sleeping baby's; if you notice bracing in the jaw, the shoulders or the hands, let that one place go. When a thought pulls you away, come back to the hand rising and falling.

wordCard.voice: Like an infant. Chapter ten's picture for a breath that isn't bracing against anything, and a life that gives without holding on. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from the Tao Te Ching: an infant, a baby. Chapter ten asks if the breath can become soft like one.

carryVoice: Your line: soft breath. Nothing to fix, only something to let go of. See you at chapter eleven.
